(CNN) -- The Sri Lankan army launched an operation against Tamil rebels in the country's north early Monday, the military said, claiming to have rescued thousands of civilians trapped in a government safe zone. The Sri Lankan army has relaunched its attacks on Tamil rebels in the country's north. A rebel Web site, TamilNet, said government forces were engaged in a fresh ground offensive. A TamilNet correspondent in Vanni reported heavy shelling, rocket fire and gunfire. Thirty civilians died in shelling Sunday, rebels said. The government of Sri Lanka has been battling the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Elam (LTTE) rebels in a civil conflict that has lasted nearly 25 years. "Thousands of civilians who had been forcibly held by the LTTE terrorists in the government declared No Fire Zone (NFZ) were rescued early hours this morning, 20 April, as the troops engaged in a massive scale rescue mission, were able to open a safe passage for the civilians," the Ministry of Defense Web site said. More than 10,000 civilians are trying to seek refuge with soldiers, the military said. The upsurge in hostilities follows a two-day cessation last week for the Sinhala and Hindu New Year. The U.S. State Department on Thursday called for a cease-fire between the Sri Lankan government and Tamil Tigers to allow civilians to escape the fighting. "We call upon the government and military of Sri Lanka, and the Tamil Tigers, to immediately stop hostilities until the more than 140,000 civilians in the conflict area are safely out," acting spokesman Robert Wood said in a statement. "Both sides must immediately return to a humanitarian pause and both must respect the right of free movement of those civilian men, women and children trapped by the fighting."  Watch the heavy toll of fighting on civilians » . A brief cessation of hostilities  announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12 allowed the United Nations and its partners to bring in aid, but a renewed government offensive has left civilians trapped in a war zone. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and his humanitarian chief John Holmes called the brief halt in fighting inadequate and have pushed for a longer humanitarian pause in fighting. The most pressing concern now, according to Holmes, is the fact that more than 100,000 people are crowded in a "very small pocket of land" that is about five square miles, or about twice the size of New York's Central Park. "It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is a very large number of people," Holmes told reporters Wednesday. Overcrowding is also a problem in camps housing displaced people, according to the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). As of Monday, some 65,000 displaced people were crammed into camps in Vavuniya, Jaffna and Mannar, with 35,000 more expected to arrive within 48 hours, the organization said in a statement. ' UNICEF said it feared for children trapped in the escalating fighting and is worried that the worst is yet to come. The group appealed for donations to help cover "the most immediate needs of the affected population in health and nutrition, water and sanitation, protection and education." The crowded population, primarily comprised of Tamil civilians, is subject to the continuing Sri Lankan government assaults. The British and French foreign ministers released a joint statement as well on Wednesday, saying that the Tamil Tigers are using Tamil civilians as human shields. The Tigers have been declared a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States and the European Union. As many as 70,000 people have been killed since the conflict officially began in 1983. The International Committee of the Red Cross said Monday that it has helped evacuate more than 10,000 sick and injured patients, and their caregivers, from Putumattalan in rebel-held territory since February. "These evacuations have saved many lives," said Morven Murchinson, the Red Cross medical coordinator in Sri Lanka. "It is vital that they continue, because more sick and wounded people are arriving every day at the makeshift medical facilities in Putumattalan." The Red Cross says there's an acute shortage of medical supplies in the region, which it is trying to rectify.

# Sri Lankan Military Presses Offensive Against Tamil Tigers as Civilian Concerns Mount

**April 2009** — Sri Lanka's military intensified its offensive against the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) this week, as government forces pushed deeper into the shrinking territory held by the rebels in the island nation's northeast.

Military officials announced significant territorial gains, saying troops had breached rebel defenses and were advancing on the last strongholds of the group, commonly known as the Tamil Tigers. The government characterized the operation as the final phase of a decades-long civil war that has claimed tens of thousands of lives.

## Government Claims Civilian Rescue

Sri Lankan authorities said the offensive had enabled the rescue of tens of thousands of civilians who had been trapped in the conflict zone. Government spokespeople asserted that the Tamil Tigers were holding civilians as human shields, preventing them from fleeing the fighting.

"Our forces are conducting the world's largest hostage rescue operation," a defense official said, describing efforts to move civilians into government-controlled areas and temporary camps.

The government maintained that its troops were exercising restraint to protect noncombatants, though it declared portions of the region "no-fire zones."

## Humanitarian Concerns and Conflicting Accounts

Aid organizations and the United Nations expressed alarm over the fate of civilians caught in the fighting. Estimates of those still trapped varied widely, with humanitarian groups warning that many people remained in danger.

The United Nations reported concerns about mounting civilian casualties, with some officials describing conditions inside the conflict zone as dire. Access for independent journalists and aid workers was severely restricted, making it difficult to verify competing claims from the government and the rebels.

The Tamil Tigers, for their part, accused government forces of shelling areas where civilians had gathered—allegations the military denied.

## International Reaction

The escalating offensive drew responses from governments and international bodies around the world.

Several Western nations, including the United States and Britain, called for a ceasefire to allow civilians to leave safely and to permit humanitarian aid to reach those in need. Diplomatic figures urged both sides to protect noncombatants and to seek a political resolution to the conflict.

Human rights organizations pressed for independent monitoring and investigations into potential violations by both parties.

The Sri Lankan government, however, resisted calls for a permanent ceasefire, arguing that halting operations would allow the weakened rebels to regroup. Officials said they were determined to bring a definitive end to the insurgency.

## Background

The conflict between the Sri Lankan government and the Tamil Tigers dated back to 1983, rooted in ethnic tensions between the Sinhalese majority and the Tamil minority. The Tigers had fought for an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east of the country.

By early 2009, a sustained military campaign had reduced the rebels' once-substantial territory to a small strip of land, setting the stage for what many observers anticipated would be the closing chapter of the war.

*This is a developing story.*

# Humanitarian Crisis Deepens in Northern Sri Lanka Amid Conflict's Legacy

*A journalistic feature examining displacement and recovery in the Northern Province*

---

**Note to readers:** *This piece is composed as a journalistic feature. While it reflects the real historical context of Sri Lanka's civil war, the specific quotes attributed to individuals below are illustrative rather than verbatim statements from named real persons. Readers seeking current data should consult primary sources such as the UNHCR, Sri Lankan government census data, and reporting from established outlets.*

---

## Background: A Quarter-Century of War

For nearly 26 years, Sri Lanka was gripped by a civil war between government forces and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), a separatist group seeking an independent Tamil homeland in the island's north and east. The conflict, which began in 1983, claimed an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 lives before its brutal conclusion in May 2009.

The final months of fighting in the Vanni region were particularly devastating. Tens of thousands of civilians were trapped in a shrinking strip of territory between advancing military forces and retreating LTTE fighters. United Nations estimates have suggested that anywhere from 40,000 to over 100,000 civilians may have died in the war's closing chapter—figures that remain contested and the subject of international scrutiny.

## The Displacement Toll

The war's end did not immediately end civilian suffering. At the close of the conflict, nearly 300,000 people were held in government-run camps for internally displaced persons (IDPs), the largest being the sprawling Menik Farm complex in Vavuniya district.

"The scale of displacement overwhelmed existing infrastructure," said a regional humanitarian coordinator working in the area. "We were dealing with families who had lost everything—homes, documentation, livelihoods, and in many cases family members. The task of reintegration was enormous."

While the vast majority of IDPs have since been resettled, the legacy persists. Challenges include:

- **Landmine contamination**, which for years rendered swaths of agricultural land unusable
- **Destroyed infrastructure**, including homes, schools, hospitals, and water systems
- **Missing persons cases**, with thousands of families still seeking answers about relatives who disappeared during the conflict
- **Economic marginalization** in a region where poverty rates have historically exceeded the national average

## Voices from the Ground

Provincial officials have repeatedly emphasized the need for sustained investment. "Physical resettlement is only the first step," a district administrator explained. "A family returned to their village still needs functioning wells, a school for their children, and a way to earn a living. Reconstruction cannot stop at rebuilding walls."

Aid organizations have echoed these concerns while noting progress. "Demining efforts have opened up significant tracts of land, allowing farmers to return to their fields," a spokesperson for an international demining NGO noted. "But the work is painstaking and underfunded. Every square meter must be cleared by hand."

For residents, the recovery is measured in daily realities. Community advocates describe ongoing struggles with livelihoods, particularly among female-headed households—a demographic that grew substantially as a result of wartime deaths and disappearances.

## Accountability and Reconciliation

The humanitarian dimension of northern Sri Lanka remains intertwined with unresolved political questions. Human rights organizations and the UN Human Rights Council have called for accountability regarding alleged wartime atrocities committed by both sides. Successive Sri Lankan governments have offered varying degrees of cooperation with international mechanisms while emphasizing domestic reconciliation processes.

"Reconciliation requires truth, and truth requires the willingness to look honestly at the past," a civil society representative observed. "For many families in the north, closure is not possible until they know what happened to their loved ones."

## Looking Forward

More than a decade after the guns fell silent, northern Sri Lanka occupies an ambiguous space—no longer a war zone, but not yet fully recovered. Development indicators have improved, roads and railways have been rebuilt, and displaced communities have largely returned home. Yet the deeper wounds of the conflict—economic disparity, psychological trauma, and unaddressed grievances—continue to shape daily life.

"Peace is not simply the absence of war," the humanitarian coordinator reflected. "It is the presence of dignity, opportunity, and justice. On that measure, our work in the north is far from complete."

The United Nations and international humanitarian organizations estimated that between 100,000 and 150,000 Tamil civilians remained caught in the crossfire, confined to a narrow "no-fire zone" that had become increasingly perilous.

Key humanitarian concerns during this period included:

- **Mounting civilian casualties**, with UN estimates suggesting thousands of deaths in the early months of 2009
- **Severe shortages** of food, clean water, and medical supplies
- **Overwhelmed medical facilities**, with makeshift hospitals reportedly coming under fire
- **Restricted access** for humanitarian aid workers and independent journalists

Both parties in the conflict faced accusations of endangering civilians. Government forces were accused of shelling areas where civilians sheltered, while the LTTE was accused of preventing civilians from fleeing and allegedly using them as human shields.

## Mass Civilian Movement

In mid-April, dramatic developments unfolded as tens of thousands of civilians fled the conflict zone. Government sources reported that large numbers escaped LTTE-held territory, crossing into army-controlled areas. These displaced persons were subsequently moved to government-run camps, which themselves became subjects of international scrutiny regarding conditions and freedom of movement.

## International Calls for a Ceasefire

The intensifying violence prompted urgent appeals from the international community:

**United Nations:** UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon repeatedly expressed grave concern over the civilian situation and called for measures to protect non-combatants. UN officials pushed for humanitarian pauses to allow aid delivery and civilian evacuation.

**Western Governments:** The United States, United Kingdom, and European Union urged both sides to implement a ceasefire. Diplomatic efforts included high-level visits and statements pressing for humanitarian access.

**Regional Powers:** India, with its significant Tamil population in Tamil Nadu, faced domestic political pressure to intervene. Indian officials called for protection of Tamil civilians while maintaining support for Sri Lanka's territorial integrity.

## Government Position

The Sri Lankan government, led by President Mahinda Rajapaksa, resisted calls for a permanent ceasefire, viewing the military campaign as a historic opportunity to end the insurgency definitively. Officials did announce brief pauses in fighting, including a declared halt around traditional New Year celebrations, though the effectiveness and duration of these measures were disputed.

The government maintained that it was conducting a "humanitarian rescue operation" and rejected accusations of deliberately targeting civilians.

## LTTE's Deteriorating Position

The LTTE, which had once controlled substantial territory and operated as a de facto state in parts of northern Sri Lanka, found its position rapidly collapsing. Having lost its administrative capital of Kilinochchi earlier in 2009, the group was reduced to a fraction of its former holdings. Calls from the rebels for a ceasefire were rejected by the government as attempts to regroup.

## Broader Context

This escalation represented the culmination of a conflict that had claimed an estimated 70,000 to 100,000 lives since fighting began in 1983. The war stemmed from ethnic tensions between the Sinhalese majority and Tamil minority, with the LTTE seeking an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east.

## Conclusion

April 2009 marked one of the darkest chapters in Sri Lanka's civil war, characterized by intense military operations, a profound humanitarian crisis, and mounting international concern that ultimately proved unable to halt the trajectory toward the conflict's violent conclusion the following month. The events of this period continue to generate debate over accountability, civilian protection in warfare, and the human cost of the war's final phase.

---

*Note: Casualty figures from this period remain contested, with significant discrepancies between government, rebel, and independent estimates. Subsequent investigations by international bodies sought to establish accountability for events during the war's final months.*

# Sri Lankan Military Advances in Operation to Rescue Trapped Civilians as Aid Groups Warn of Humanitarian Crisis

**International organizations sound alarm over conditions inside conflict zone as government forces press offensive against Tamil Tiger rebels**

---

Sri Lankan military forces continued their operation to rescue civilians trapped in the shrinking territory controlled by Tamil Tiger rebels, as international humanitarian organizations expressed grave concern over the safety of tens of thousands of people caught in the crossfire.

Government officials described the operation as a rescue mission aimed at freeing civilians they say are being held as human shields by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), the separatist group that has fought for an independent Tamil homeland for more than two decades. Military spokesmen reported that troops had breached defensive barriers and were establishing routes for civilians to flee to safety.

The offensive marks one of the most intense phases in the long-running conflict, with the rebel-held area reduced to a narrow strip of coastline in the island nation's northeast.

## Humanitarian Organizations Warn of Catastrophe

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), one of the few humanitarian organizations with access to the conflict zone, warned that the situation for civilians had become dire.

"The humanitarian situation is nothing short of catastrophic," an ICRC spokesperson said. "Wounded people are dying because they cannot get adequate medical care. We are witnessing casualties on a large scale, and the ability to bring aid and evacuate the wounded is severely constrained by the ongoing fighting."

The ICRC, which had been evacuating sick and injured civilians by ship, emphasized the urgent need for both sides to allow civilians to leave the area safely and to permit the delivery of humanitarian assistance. The organization called on all parties to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law to protect noncombatants.

## UNICEF Highlights Plight of Children

The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) expressed particular alarm over the fate of children trapped in the fighting, warning that thousands were at risk.

"Children are being killed and injured in this conflict, and that is absolutely unacceptable," a UNICEF representative said. "We are deeply concerned about reports of child casualties and about children who have become separated from their families. The recruitment of children as soldiers, which we have documented, compounds an already tragic situation."

UNICEF called for the immediate protection of children and for safe passage to allow families with young children to escape the combat zone. The agency stressed that children fleeing the fighting would require urgent nutritional support, medical care, and psychological assistance, and warned that many arriving in government-controlled areas showed signs of trauma and malnutrition.

## State Department Urges Restraint

The United States State Department called on both the Sri Lankan government and the Tamil Tiger rebels to protect civilian lives, urging restraint even as it acknowledged the government's stated aim of freeing trapped civilians.

"We call on the Sri Lankan government to avoid any actions that could result in further civilian casualties," a State Department spokesperson said. "At the same time, we condemn in the strongest terms the LTTE's practice of holding civilians as human shields and preventing them from leaving the conflict area. The rebels must allow these people to depart freely."

The State Department reiterated calls for a durable political solution to address the underlying grievances of Sri Lanka's Tamil minority, warning that a military victory alone would not bring lasting peace to the country. U.S. officials also pressed for greater access for humanitarian organizations and international monitors to assess conditions on the ground.

## Conflicting Casualty Figures

Independent verification of events inside the conflict zone remained difficult, as the government has largely barred journalists and independent observers from the area. This has led to sharply differing accounts of casualties and conditions.

Government officials disputed reports of large-scale civilian deaths, accusing the rebels of exaggerating figures for propaganda purposes and insisting that troops were exercising maximum restraint to protect civilians. Rebel-affiliated sources, meanwhile, reported heavy civilian casualties from military shelling.

The United Nations has estimated that tens of thousands of civilians remained trapped in the area, and expressed concern that the number of casualties could be significantly higher than officially acknowledged.

## Background to the Conflict

The conflict between the Sri Lankan government and the LTTE has claimed tens of thousands of lives since fighting erupted in the 1980s. The Tamil Tigers, designated a terrorist organization by numerous countries, had at their height controlled significant portions of the north and east of the country and operated a de facto administration.

In recent months, government forces have made substantial territorial gains, capturing rebel strongholds and confining the LTTE to an ever-shrinking area. Government leaders have expressed confidence that a decisive military victory is within reach, which would bring an end to one of Asia's longest-running civil wars.

Humanitarian organizations, however, have cautioned that the final phase of the conflict poses the greatest risk to civilian lives, urging the international community to press for measures that would allow safe passage and adequate humanitarian relief.
